questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Limits and Derivatives / Limits and the definition of the derivative
questions.solution:
A polynomial has no break anywhere, so its limit at a point is simply its value there. Substitute:
$$\lim_{x \to 4}(2x-3)=2 \times 4-3=5.$$
distractorRationale: Kept the constant term alone and ignored the $2x$ part.
Read off the coefficient of $x$ rather than evaluating the whole expression.
Correct. Substituting $x=4$ gives $8-3=5$.
Stopped at $2 \times 4$ and never subtracted the $3$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Limits and Derivatives / Limits and the definition of the derivative
questions.solution:
Putting $x=-2$ straight in makes both parts vanish, so the fraction has to be simplified before it can be read.

Factorise the top and cancel the shared bracket:
$$\frac{x^{2}-4}{x+2}=\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x+2}=x-2, \qquad x \neq -2.$$

What is left is a polynomial, and a limit never asks about the point itself, only about values nearby. Substitute:
$$\lim_{x \to -2}(x-2)=-2-2=-4.$$
distractorRationale: Correct. Cancelling leaves $x-2$, and $-2-2=-4$.
Reported the value $x$ moves towards instead of the value the fraction moves towards.
Cancelled down to $x+2$ rather than $x-2$, and that bracket does vanish at $x=-2$.
Subtracted in the wrong order, working out $2-(-2)$ in place of $-2-2$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Limits and Derivatives / Limits and the definition of the derivative
questions.solution:
This quotient is the definition of $f'(2)$: it measures the steepness of the curve at $x=2$, not its height.

Expand the top:
$$(2+h)^{3}-8=12h+6h^{2}+h^{3}.$$

Every term carries an $h$, so the division goes through cleanly:
$$\frac{12h+6h^{2}+h^{3}}{h}=12+6h+h^{2}.$$

As $h$ shrinks to $0$ the last two terms die away, leaving $12$.
distractorRationale: Lowered the exponent without bringing the $3$ down, then evaluated $2^{2}$.
Read off the coefficient of the $6h$ term, which vanishes once $h$ shrinks to zero.
This is $f(2)=8$, the height of the curve at that point rather than its steepness.
Correct. The quotient simplifies to $12+6h+h^{2}$, whose value at $h=0$ is $12$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Limits and Derivatives / Differentiation rules and tangent lines
questions.solution:
Differentiate one term at a time. The power rule turns $x^{k}$ into $kx^{k-1}$: the exponent drops in front as a multiplier and then falls by one.

For $x^{3}$, the $3$ comes down and the exponent becomes $2$, giving $3x^{2}$.

For $-4x$, the exponent is $1$, so it drops to $0$ and the term becomes the constant $-4$.
$$f'(x)=3x^{2}-4.$$
distractorRationale: Differentiated the cubic term but copied $-4x$ across untouched.
Correct. $x^{3}$ becomes $3x^{2}$ and $-4x$ becomes $-4$.
Lowered the exponent but forgot to bring the $3$ down in front of it.
Deleted the linear term. Its derivative is the constant $-4$, not zero.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Limits and Derivatives / Differentiation rules and tangent lines
questions.stem: A tangent to the curve $y=x^{2}-5x+3$ runs parallel to the line $y=3x-1$. At which $x$ does it touch the curve?
questions.solution:
Parallel lines share a slope, so the tangent has slope $3$.

The steepness of the curve at any $x$ is
$$y'=2x-5.$$

Set that equal to $3$ and solve:
$$2x-5=3, \qquad 2x=8, \qquad x=4.$$
distractorRationale: Moved the $-5$ across without changing its sign, solving $2x=3-5$.
Ignored the $-5$ altogether and solved $2x=3$.
Correct. $2x-5=3$ gives $x=4$.
Lost the factor $2$ from the power rule and solved $x-5=3$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Limits and Derivatives / Differentiation rules and tangent lines
questions.stem: Find the tangent to $y=x^{3}-3x$ at the point where $x=2$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — where the line touches.** At $x=2$ the curve sits at $y=8-6=2$, so the point of contact is $(2,\ 2)$.

**Step 2 — how steep it is there.** Differentiating, $y'=3x^{2}-3$, and at $x=2$ that comes to $12-3=9$.

**Step 3 — assemble the line.** Through $(2,\ 2)$ with slope $9$:
$$y-2=9(x-2), \qquad\text{so}\qquad y=9x-16.$$
distractorRationale: Used the height $2$ as the slope. Height and steepness are two different readings of the same curve.
Correct. Slope $9$ through $(2,\ 2)$ gives $y-2=9(x-2)$, that is $y=9x-16$.
Wrote $y=9(x-2)$ and never added the height $2$ back on.
Treated $2$ as the intercept, as though the contact point sat on the $y$-axis.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Limits and Derivatives / Monotonicity and extrema using derivatives
questions.solution:
A curve falls exactly where its derivative is negative.
$$f'(x)=3x^{2}-12=3(x^{2}-4).$$

Solve $3(x^{2}-4)<0$. Dividing by the positive $3$ leaves
$$x^{2}<4, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad -2<x<2.$$

Outside that band $x^{2}>4$, the derivative is positive and the curve climbs. So the only falling stretch is $(-2,\ 2)$.
distractorRationale: This is one of the two climbing stretches, where $f'>0$.
The other climbing stretch. Both tails rise, because $f'(x)>0$ once $|x|>2$.
Read $x^{2}<4$ as $-4<x<4$, forgetting to take the square root of the $4$.
Correct. $f'(x)<0$ precisely when $x^{2}<4$, which is the interval $(-2,\ 2)$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Limits and Derivatives / Monotonicity and extrema using derivatives
questions.stem: Find the local minimum value of $f(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+5$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — find the turning points.**
$$f'(x)=3x^{2}-12x=3x(x-4),$$
which is zero at $x=0$ and at $x=4$.

**Step 2 — say which is which.** $f'$ is positive to the left of $0$, negative between $0$ and $4$, and positive again beyond $4$. The curve therefore drops into $x=4$ and rises out of it, making $x=4$ the minimum; $x=0$ is the maximum.

**Step 3 — evaluate there.** A minimum *value* is a height, so substitute back:
$$f(4)=64-96+5=-27.$$
distractorRationale: Correct. The turning point at $x=4$ is the minimum, and $f(4)=-27$.
Used $x=2$, the midpoint of the two turning points, where the curve is still on its way down.
Reported the position $x=4$ rather than the height of the curve there.
This is $f(0)=5$, the local maximum. The other turning point was chosen.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Limits and Derivatives / Monotonicity and extrema using derivatives
questions.stem: The function $f(x)=x^{3}+ax^{2}+3x$ is increasing on the whole of $\mathbb{R}$. Find the range of $a$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — turn the wording into a condition.** Increasing everywhere means $f'(x) \ge 0$ for every real $x$, where
$$f'(x)=3x^{2}+2ax+3.$$

**Step 2 — a parabola that never dips below the axis.** The leading coefficient $3$ is positive, so this parabola opens upwards. It stays at or above the axis exactly when it has no two distinct roots, that is when its discriminant is at most zero:
$$(2a)^{2}-4 \times 3 \times 3 \le 0, \qquad 4a^{2} \le 36, \qquad a^{2} \le 9.$$

**Step 3 — read off the bounds.** $a^{2} \le 9$ means $-3 \le a \le 3$.

The ends are kept. At $a=\pm 3$ the derivative touches zero at a single point and is positive elsewhere, and one isolated zero does not interrupt the climb.
distractorRationale: Threw the ends away. At $a=\pm 3$ the derivative only grazes zero at one point, so those two values are still allowed.
Correct. $f' \ge 0$ everywhere forces $4a^{2}-36 \le 0$, giving $-3 \le a \le 3$.
Quoted $9$ as the bound, reading it straight from $a^{2} \le 9$ without taking the square root.
Solved the discriminant condition the wrong way round, using $4a^{2}-36 \ge 0$.
